Editorial rewrite of advisor and client prose; substance unchanged.

advisor.summary: The TCJA opened the cash method to nearly every small business, and the ceiling indexes upward each year: a taxpayer that meets the §448(c) gross-receipts test — a $32 million three-year average for 2026, computed with aggregation — may use the cash method even with inventories, and the same test lifts §263A UNICAP and full §471 inventory accounting. For the typical service or B2B accrual client whose receivables run ahead of payables, the switch defers the entire net receivable position: a favorable §481(a) catch-up, deducted in full in the change year on an automatic Form 3115. This record is advisory because the payoff is a balance-sheet fact — net A/R over A/P at the change date — that the engine does not carry; quantify it from the books before quoting a number.
mechanics: Eligibility turns on §448(c): three-year average gross receipts at or below the indexed ceiling ($32 million for 2026), aggregating commonly controlled entities under §448(c)(2); a syndicate allocating more than 35 percent of losses to limited owners is excluded no matter its size.

On the cash method, income counts when actually or constructively received and deductions when paid, so receivables sit untaxed until collected — the deferral lives in the gap against the accrual all-events test.

The same receipts test opens §471(c) inventory relief — treat inventory as non-incidental materials and supplies or follow the books — and the §263A(i) UNICAP exemption, which ends indirect-cost capitalization.

The change is automatic: Form 3115 under the Rev. Proc. 2015-13 procedures, filed with the timely return, no user fee, audit protection for prior years; the §481(a) adjustment sweeps in the cumulative difference — deducted in full in the change year when negative, spread over four years when positive.

Direction matters: cash wins where receivables exceed payables plus accrued liabilities; accrual can win for deposit-heavy businesses, because a cash-method taxpayer picks up customer deposits as income the moment they arrive.

authority.note: Cash-method eligibility via the aggregated gross-receipts test — a $32 million average for 2026, indexed annually — plus the tax-shelter exclusion.
Small-business inventory options that stand in for full inventory accounting.
UNICAP exemption tied to the same receipts test.
The one-time cumulative catch-up that lands the deferral in the change year.
Automatic method-change procedures: Form 3115 filed with the timely return, audit protection, and the rules for deducting negative adjustments and spreading positive ones.

requirements: Aggregated three-year average gross receipts at or below the indexed ceiling, and the syndicate screen cleared.
A balance-sheet snapshot as of the proposed change date: receivables, payables, accrued liabilities, customer deposits, and inventory.
Comfort with cash-basis tax numbers — lenders can still receive accrual financials; the two systems coexist.
risks: The benefit is deferral, not forgiveness: receivables are taxed as collected, growth compounds the benefit, and contraction quietly unwinds it.
Outgrowing the receipts ceiling forces a change back to accrual with a positive §481(a) adjustment — model the exit for growth clients before making the entrance.
Deposit-heavy businesses can fare worse on cash: advance payments are income on receipt, while accrual taxpayers keep a deferral path.
Aggregation errors void eligibility — counting related entities separately is the classic failure.
A method is not a dial: it is adopted consistently and changed only with consent — no year-by-year cherry-picking.
stateNotes: Conformity: states that start from federal taxable income or federal AGI conform to the method and to the §481(a) adjustment as computed federally; confirm any state-specific addback rules across the client's filing footprint.
PTET interaction: the change-year catch-up deduction shrinks the entity income on which a pass-through entity tax election is computed, so reset PTET estimates in the change year.

Missouri: conforms through rolling IRC conformity and its federal starting points (RSMo §143.091, §143.431), and an entity electing under the Missouri SALT Parity Act (RSMo §143.436) computes the PTET on the post-adjustment income.

client.teaser: One accounting election can move a whole year of unpaid invoices off this year's tax bill.
client.headline: Stop paying tax on invoices before the cash comes in
plainEnglish: There are two ways to keep score for taxes. The accrual way counts income when you send the invoice. The cash way counts income when the money lands in your bank. If customers owe you a lot at any moment, the accrual way makes you pay tax ahead of your own cash.

Most businesses under $32 million in sales may switch to the cash method. The switch brings a one-time reward. All the billed-but-unpaid income you were already taxed on gets subtracted in the year you change. If customers owe you $200,000 more than you owe suppliers, that is roughly a $200,000 deduction.

To be clear, this is a deferral. Those dollars are taxed when they come in. But the benefit rolls forward as long as the business keeps its scale, and we can time the switch to a high-income year, when it is worth the most.
client.analogy: It is the difference between being taxed on your order book and being taxed on your cash register. The register is the honest measure of what you can actually spend.
benefits: A potentially large one-time deduction in the year you switch
No more tax on money customers have not paid yet
Often ends heavy inventory accounting at the same time
steps: WE confirm you qualify, counting related companies the way the IRS requires.
WE compute your exact one-time deduction from the balance sheet.
WE pick the best year and file the single form that makes it official.
YOU keep sending us year-end financials so we can watch the sales ceiling.
